records.sourceFile: Acupuncture and dry needling for sports performance and recovery.pdf

paper.citation: Tang CT, Song B. Acupuncture and Dry Needling for Sports Performance and Recovery. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2022;21(6):213-218.
paper.abstract: Acupuncture and dry needling share mechanisms and sports medicine applications. Pain is the most common indication, but there are limited studies on ergogenic use. Needling may improve muscular strength and power, including jump height, and flexibility. For recovery, acupuncture can relieve pain after injury and may help delayed-onset muscle soreness. There are many case reports in athletes, but more high-quality studies are needed for specific evidence-based recommendations. Given the high safety and few adverse events, needling can likely be promoted in athletes.
paper.tldr: Needling has a good safety record in athletes and may help soreness and flexibility, but the evidence for strength and power gains is small and mixed, and the review finds no clear aerobic benefit. Use it as a low-risk adjunct, not a proven performance aid.
paper.methods: A narrative review by two physicians in physical medicine and rehabilitation, summarizing acupuncture and dry needling research on performance (strength, power, endurance, flexibility) and recovery (muscle soreness). The article describes proposed mechanisms, cites randomized trials, case series, a systematic review of case reports in athletes, and a meta-analysis of DOMS trials, and includes perceptual interview data from track and field athletes. No search method is described.
paper.findings: Most studies reported improved muscle performance after acupuncture, and differences from sham appeared mainly when the sham did not penetrate the skin; for example, 20 healthy men improved average max torque and power after true acupuncture against a blunt-needle sham, while in 32 female students both true and shallow-needle sham groups improved from baseline, with larger gains after true acupuncture. A meta-analysis of six RCTs (210 participants) found acupuncture reduced soreness (SMD -0.49) and creatine kinase (SMD -0.91) and improved strength (SMD -0.54) after intense exercise. In 62 marathon runners, postrace dry needling did not reduce cramping and increased soleus soreness on days 1 and 2, and in one study needling increased hip flexion range but decreased quadriceps strength.
paper.limitations: The review describes no search strategy or inclusion criteria, and it draws on small single-session trials, uncontrolled studies, case reports and sham controls of varying quality, with the Lee et al. systematic review covering case reports only. The authors note that needling effects are partly nonspecific and that mechanisms are largely theoretical.
paper.practicalImplications: Needling can be considered as a low-risk adjunct for delayed-onset soreness after strenuous exercise, where the meta-analysis suggests a modest reduction, but one marathon trial found postrace dry needling increased calf soreness. Short-term range of motion gains were reported, but one study also found reduced quadriceps strength afterward, so needling just before testing or competition is not supported. It is not supported as a training method to raise strength or power, and it did not prevent cramps.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the evidence for strength, power and endurance gains is small, short-term and mixed. Torque or force gains were seen right after single sessions in healthy adults, students and a small group of Division III athletes, and aerobic benefits are not convincing. Staff should not plan needling as a training stimulus on this evidence.
paper.rtp: Limited. The review includes injured athletes and case reports of pain relief, but the return-to-play evidence is case-based or from small trials without standard return-to-sport criteria. It cannot be used to set return-to-play timing or to show that needling speeds return to sport, although athletes in one interview study valued the possibility of a quicker return.

records.sourceFile: Effects of Nightly Electronic Device Restriction and Morning Bright Light on Sleep, Mood, and Performance Among Elite Athletes (1).pdf

paper.citation: Hoshikawa M. Effects of nightly electronic device restriction and morning bright light on sleep, mood, and performance among elite athletes. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025;39(11):1155-1162.
paper.abstract: Twenty-five elite athletes were divided into an intervention group (n=12), who turned off electronic devices 30 minutes before bed and had 20 minutes of morning bright light (about 10,000 lux), and a control group (n=13). Sleep, sleepiness, mood and performance were monitored over 2 weeks. The intervention group improved POMS vigor, reaction time, rebound jump height and rebound jump index without a change in sleep parameters. Epworth sleepiness and squat jump changes were not significant between groups.
paper.tldr: Two weeks of stopping device use 30 minutes before bed and 20 minutes of morning bright light was followed by better mood, reaction time and rebound jump performance in elite athletes compared with controls. Sleep did not change, and the sample was small with baseline differences in jump performance.
paper.methods: Randomised controlled trial in 25 elite athletes (24 international, 11 men, 14 women) from 12 sports, allocated to intervention (n=12) or control (n=13), after 13 of 38 initially randomised athletes were excluded for pain, injury, illness or schedule reasons. Over 2 weeks, actigraphy, Karolinska sleepiness, subjective sleep quality, fatigue and morning heart rate were recorded daily. Before and after, Epworth sleepiness, POMS, psychomotor vigilance reaction time, grip strength, squat and rebound jumps, and exercise heart rate were measured and analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests.
paper.findings: In the intervention group, POMS vigor rose from 14.6 to 25.9, reaction time fell from 240 to 225 ms, rebound jump height rose from 28.6 to 30.6 cm and rebound jump index from 1.56 to 1.73, with significant group by day interactions (p=0.042, 0.032, 0.031 and 0.017). Epworth sleepiness, POMS fatigue and left grip strength improved within both groups with no significant interaction, so those gains were not specific to the intervention. Actigraphy sleep measures did not change in either group, and the intervention group had a wider range of wake times during the study (earliest wake 5:35 vs 6:23, p=0.012).
paper.limitations: Small sample and post hoc power of 0.68, so type II error is likely. Thirteen athletes were excluded after random assignment. The intervention group had lower baseline rebound jump height (p<0.01) and index (p<0.05) than controls, so part of the improvement may reflect catch-up. Training could not be controlled, self-reported data came from a non-blinded design, and actigraphy was missing for one intervention athlete. The abstract gives p=0.016 for the within-group reaction time change, while Table 3 gives p=0.001; the table value is used here.
paper.practicalImplications: In elite athletes with irregular sleep schedules, a two-week routine of stopping device use 30 minutes before bed and 20 minutes of morning bright light was followed by better mood, faster reaction times and better rebound jump performance. Staff should not expect it to change measured sleep, and the author recommends a device rather than self-report to assess sleep regularity, because measured irregularity was larger than reported.
paper.athleteDev: The protocol can be considered as a low-burden way to support alertness and mood around training, but the evidence comes from 25 athletes and several outcomes did not differ from controls. Because sleep did not change, the benefit should not be described as better sleep.
paper.rtp: The athletes were not injured and return to sport was not assessed. The study cannot be used to decide readiness to return to play or to guide rehabilitation timelines.

records.sourceFile: Optimizing athletes' recovery and performance - A review of vibration therapy, compression garments, and massage.pdf

paper.citation: Chen J, Cogburn J, Marcussen B, Slayman T. Optimizing Athletes' Recovery and Performance: A Review of Vibration Therapy, Compression Garments, and Massage. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2025;24(6):177-185.
paper.abstract: Vibration therapy, massage and compression garments are increasingly common recovery modalities for amateur and elite athletes. The authors reviewed PubMed studies on their effects on performance and recovery, identifying 29 eligible vibration, 31 compression and 25 massage articles. The modalities had varying support, all appeared safe, and the authors call for standardized protocols to define the best duration and frequency.
paper.tldr: A PubMed-based review finding that massage and vibration reduce soreness and pain in many studies, while compression garments show weak support. Performance benefits were inconsistent for all three, and all three appear safe, but results vary by outcome and protocol.
paper.methods: Literature review of PubMed records from the earliest date to May 1, 2022, using terms including massage, vibration, compression garment and muscle soreness. Inclusion was limited to English-language journal articles from 2000 onward, screened by title and abstract, with systematic and meta-analytic reviews used to identify original studies. Each outcome was classified as significantly improved, not significant, or significantly worse.
paper.findings: Massage reduced pain or DOMS in 17 of 19 studies, reduced CK or myoglobin in all 3 studies that measured them, and improved strength in 5 of 10 studies. Vibration reduced pain or DOMS in 17 of 22 studies and CK or myoglobin in 7 of 12 studies, but improved strength in only 6 of 15 studies and showed no clear performance benefit. Compression garments reduced pain in 16 of 29 studies, swelling in 8 of 13, and CK or myoglobin in 5 of 17, while 12 of 17 CK or myoglobin studies and all 8 inflammatory marker studies found no difference. Although 8 of 12 compression strength studies found improvement, only 1 of 11 sports performance studies did, and the authors concluded there was no clear performance or range-of-motion benefit.
paper.limitations: The review uses one database and no described quality appraisal, and included studies differed in design, sample size (8 to 220), protocol and participant training level. The authors state that there are no long-term studies and that publication bias may favor positive findings. Several outcome groups have very few studies, such as only two inflammatory marker studies for massage.
paper.practicalImplications: Massage and vibration can be used to ease perceived soreness after hard training, but performance gains from either are not consistently shown. Compression garments should be seen as a way to reduce perceived pain rather than a proven recovery tool. Authors note that massage of 5-12 minutes appeared sufficient in one cited meta-analysis, and that several minutes of vibration may help strength while longer sessions may reduce it. Use the same protocol and track soreness and performance over time so the response can be judged.
paper.athleteDev: Use massage or vibration to manage soreness and comfort between sessions, but do not count on them to improve strength or sprint performance. For compression garments, the review supports pain relief only. Keep the protocol consistent and record pain and performance outcomes so the athlete's response is clear.
paper.rtp: The included studies mainly induced soreness or muscle damage with exercise in healthy or trained people and did not test injured athletes. The review does not report injury, rehabilitation or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot be used to judge when an injured athlete can return to sport. The authors' comment that less pain may help athletes return to training sooner is about training, not return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Slow wave sleep - a recovery period after exercise.pdf

paper.citation: Shapiro CM, Bortz R, Mitchell D, Bartel P, Jooste P. Slow-Wave Sleep: A Recovery Period After Exercise. Science. 1981;214:1253-1254.
paper.abstract: Sleep was recorded in athletes on four successive nights after a 92 km road race and compared with control nights. Total sleep time and slow-wave sleep both increased after this metabolic stress.
paper.tldr: After a 92 km marathon, six young runners slept longer than on control nights on all four nights recorded and had more slow-wave sleep on the first two. Because it is one extreme event in six athletes, the result shows a sleep response to a very large load, not that sleep speeds recovery.
paper.methods: Six athletes aged 18 to 26 completed a 92 km road marathon. Their sleep was recorded in a sleep laboratory on the night of the race and on three following nights, and compared with the mean of one pre-race control night two weeks before the race (after an unrecorded adaptation night) and one post-race control night two weeks after it. Records were scored blind by two trained scorers, and analysis of variance compared the post-race nights with control.
paper.findings: Total sleep time was longer than control on each of the four nights after the marathon (F(4,20) = 21.3, P < .05). Slow-wave sleep as a percentage of sleep increased on nights 1 and 2 (F(4,20) = 44.0, P < .001), mainly from stage 4 on night 1, while REM sleep decreased and sleep onset to stage 2 was shorter on night 1. The authors report no significant change in slow-wave sleep percentage on nights 3 and 4.
paper.limitations: Only six athletes were studied, and although an adaptation night preceded the pre-race control, none was possible before the marathon night or run before the post-race control, so a first-night effect cannot be fully excluded; the authors used a constant 2-week interval to partly compensate. The subjects were training regularly before the race and had restarted exercising by the post-race control, so training status changed between control and test nights. The paper does not show whether smaller training loads raise slow-wave sleep, and the authors note that unfit subjects in earlier studies did not show the usual increase after exercise.
paper.practicalImplications: After a very long endurance event, these athletes slept longer for four nights and had more deep sleep for about two nights, so expect that response and plan recovery around it. The study does not show that the extra sleep speeds recovery, and it gives no sleep target for training.
paper.athleteDev: The findings are consistent with deep sleep being part of recovery after very large endurance loads, which can inform how sleep is protected in the days after a long event. Performance recovery was not measured, so the study does not show a training benefit.
paper.rtp: The study does not inform return to sport. It studied endurance runners without injury data and measured no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcome.

records.sourceFile: The Relationship Between Relative Rest and Team Performance Across Competitive Seasons in the National Football League.pdf

paper.citation: Pinzone AG, Abu-Amara Y, Gant RW, Rivera J, Tagesen EC, Barkley JE, et al. The Relationship Between Relative Rest and Team Performance Across Competitive Seasons in the National Football League. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025.
paper.abstract: This study analyzed all NFL regular-season games from 1970-71 to 2022-23 to test whether relative rest between opponents is related to team win/loss ratio. The relationship was trivial and negative, and win/loss ratio did not differ across rest categories. Teams that lost in the divisional round or won the Super Bowl had lower average relative rest than teams that missed the playoffs, and the authors conclude that relative rest has no significant effect on team performance.
paper.tldr: Across 52 NFL seasons, the rest advantage a team had over its opponent had only a trivial link to win/loss ratio. Teams that lost in the divisional round or won the Super Bowl had less favorable rest than non-playoff teams, so schedule rest is unlikely to be a strong driver of team results.
paper.methods: Regular-season game records were taken from pro-football-reference.com and spot-checked against NFL.com. Relative rest index (RRI) was calculated for each game as the difference in days since each team's previous game, then averaged by team and season. Pearson correlations tested RRI against win/loss ratio, and one-way ANOVAs compared win/loss ratio across eight RRI categories and RRI across six playoff-depth categories. RRI was calculated in Eastern time without time-zone adjustment, and week 1 was set to zero for all teams.
paper.findings: Across all 12,290 games, season-average RRI had a trivial negative correlation with win/loss ratio (r = -0.064, P = 0.011, R2 = 0.004). Win/loss ratio did not differ across RRI categories (P = 0.233). RRI differed by playoff depth (P = 0.018, partial eta squared = 0.009): teams that did not make the playoffs had higher RRI than teams that lost in the divisional round (P = 0.001) or won the Super Bowl (P = 0.040).
paper.limitations: The analysis uses team-level archival records with no player, injury, practice or recovery data, and the authors name team skill, injuries and recovery strategies as possible confounders. The effect sizes are very small (R2 = 0.004 and partial eta squared = 0.009). The abstract says RRI was lower for teams that lost in the Super Bowl and divisional round, while the Results report the Super Bowl winners, and this summary uses the Results. The authors' earlier 2022-season analysis reported a larger positive correlation (r = 0.339), which this study does not replicate.
paper.practicalImplications: Across 52 NFL seasons, the rest advantage between opponents did not meaningfully change team win/loss ratio, so the league's schedule configuration does not appear to have strong effects on team results. The authors still advise that player recovery from practice and competition should not be underprioritized given the demands of a season.
paper.athleteDev: Relative rest between opponents should not be used to predict team results. The study does not measure individual readiness, workload or recovery, so it gives no guidance on athlete-level recovery planning.
paper.rtp: The study measures team win/loss ratio and playoff depth, not injury, return to play or individual recovery, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

paper.citation: Patel K, Bakshi N, Freehill MT, Awan TM. Whole-Body Cryotherapy in Sports Medicine. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2019;18(4):136-140.
paper.abstract: Reviews whole-body cryotherapy in sports medicine, covering its proposed use for injury prevention and for reducing inflammation after exercise, its physiological effects, safety and contraindications, and clinical use.
paper.tldr: Whole-body cryotherapy shows anti-inflammatory and lipid marker effects, but trials of functional recovery and performance are few and split between benefit and no benefit. The authors suggest using it only as a supplement to recovery in people without contraindications, under skilled supervision.
paper.methods: Narrative literature review. The article does not describe a search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal.
paper.findings: Pre-exercise WBC prevented IL-6 spikes in volleyball players, and repeated twice-daily sessions gave a 60% TNF decrease versus 35% with passive recovery. Creatine kinase results are mixed (a 34% decrease in kayakers and lower values in rugby players, but no difference in trained runners), and hemoglobin fell transiently in some groups but not others. Lipid profiles improved in physically active and overweight men in mostly uncontrolled studies. For function, positive trials reported better strength, pain and fatigue after trail running, better tennis shot accuracy, and better acute recovery in swimmers and endurance runners, while a 36-person trial, a systematic review of four laboratory RCTs and a crossover study found no clear benefit beyond lower soreness in one.
paper.limitations: No search method or quality appraisal is described. Most studies are small, many are uncontrolled or laboratory-based, and exposure protocols vary in temperature and duration. Some citations in the text do not match the reference list (for example, the kayaker creatine kinase study is cited to a rugby recovery paper). The authors state that a definite clinical benefit is not established and high-quality research is needed.
paper.practicalImplications: WBC should be given only with skilled supervision and after screening for contraindications, such as Raynaud disease, cold intolerance, uncontrolled hypertension, cardiovascular disease and claustrophobia; blood pressure rises during cold exposure, and aortic dissection and transient global amnesia have been reported. The authors suggest it as a supplement to functional recovery, not a replacement for other recovery methods. Expect inconsistent effects on creatine kinase and hemoglobin.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not establish a performance benefit from whole-body cryotherapy. Some trials report better tennis shot accuracy or faster acute recovery in endurance athletes, but others found no effect on strength, power or soreness, so effects should be judged individually.
paper.rtp: No return-to-sport trials are reported. In one randomized trial in adhesive capsulitis, WBC plus physical therapy improved pain, function and range of motion more than physical therapy alone after four weeks, and arthritis data come from an uncontrolled series and a systematic review. These are non-athlete clinical populations, so the review cannot set return-to-play criteria.
